frase_gancho.texto: It is called that, but no one has been able to prove that Malinche ever wore it.

puente_narrativo.texto: And so the tour ends. As you leave, look once more at the water falling from the Umbrella and remember Tláloc at the entrance. Rain, maize, the word, and thread are what join all of these halls.

guion_corto.texto: It is known as Malinche’s huipil, but no one has been able to prove that Cortés’s interpreter ever wore it. The name comes from its resemblance to garments drawn in codices such as the Tlaxcala Cloth, where she appears. Carbon fourteen studies place it much later, between the late seventeenth and the eighteenth century. It is made of three panels woven on a backstrap loom, in white and brown cotton. It has wool and silk embroidery, and threads twisted with feathers. On the front it displays a double-headed eagle, a symbol of European origin, alongside diamonds, stepped-fret patterns, and flowers. It is a unique garment: it joins the Indigenous technique of feather work with elements that arrived with the Spaniards. Because of the extreme fragility of its ancient feathers and threads, the original is kept under strict conservation conditions and is displayed only during special periods or by means of a facsimile.

guion_largo.texto:
In 1910, a newspaper asked whether this garment had belonged to Malinche. An ethnologist from the museum answered: “Perhaps so.” More than a century later, the question is still alive, and the answer tells a good story.

Let us begin with her. Malintzin, or Malinalli, was a Nahua woman who served as an interpreter and a link between Hernán Cortés and the peoples of ancient Mexico. Malinche is the Hispanicized form of her name. You may remember the malinalli sign, the grass, on the forehead of the [Malinaltepec Mask](mna_s10_mascara_malinaltepec): it was also the name of a day in the calendar. For centuries she was blamed for helping the Spaniards, and today historians debate her role more carefully.

Why was the huipil attributed to her? Because of a resemblance. In the Tlaxcala Cloth, a sixteenth-century codex, a woman wearing a similar garment appears next to Cortés. Similar garments can be seen in other codices, such as the Florentine Codex. That is why people thought it was hers. That is how it got its name.

The analyses say something else. Carbon fourteen studies, carried out between 1996 and 1998, place the garment between the late seventeenth and the early eighteenth century. That is more than a century after Malintzin’s lifetime. That is why today we speak of a huipil “attributed” to Malinche, not of a huipil that was hers. The exact date is still under study, with datings that range from the late 17th century to the late 18th.

That does not take away from its value. On the contrary, it is a very rare piece. It is made of three panels woven on a backstrap loom with white cotton and brown cotton, called coyuchi, and joined with vertical seams. It has embroidery and brocade in wool and silk, with colors of cochineal red and purple snail dye. It also has threads twisted with feathers, a pre-Hispanic technique that almost disappeared. On the front it carries a double-headed eagle, a symbol that came from Europe. In a single garment, the backstrap loom, wool, silk, and the two-headed eagle live side by side.

Its modern history also has its chapters. According to the museum’s deputy director of Ethnography, it appeared in the late nineteenth century in a market in Puebla and came into the museum around 1902. In 1910, during the celebrations of the centennial of Independence, its exhibition was announced. In 2011 it was shown in the exhibition “Wings of the Indigenous World” and was afterward put away to protect it. It has been restored, because its condition is delicate.

Because the original is so fragile, since 2019 its composition has been studied in order to make a replica. Indigenous artisans worked on it with cotton, wool, silk, plants, and traditional pigments. In September 2024 it was shown at the Xalapa Museum of Anthropology. Whether what you see here is the original garment or its copy, the label will tell you.

Before you leave, look at it once more. It is a garment that bears the name of a woman who perhaps never touched it. Even so, it tells us something true. Under Spanish rule, Indigenous weavers kept doing what was theirs and blended it with what was new. As in this entire hall, here the thread holds memory.

texto: Find the double-headed eagle embroidered on the front
Count the vertical strips that make up the garment: can you see the seams?
Notice the two tones of the cotton, white and brown

texto.Material: White cotton and coyuchi woven on a backstrap loom, embroidered with wool, silk, and feathered thread; dyes of cochineal, indigo, and purple snail
texto.Conservation: Restricted rotating display for textile preservation

texto.pregunta: Myth: This huipil was worn by Malinche, Hernán Cortés’s interpreter.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is called that because of its resemblance to garments in the codices, but studies date it more than a century after her lifetime.
